author: Brian Hioe
title: Batanes Claims Show Chinese Nationalism’s Irredentist Streak
content:
CLAIMS BY Chinese scholars that Batanes, which constitutes the smallest province of the Philippines, belongs to China were widely circulated in Philippine media last month. In particular, the claims were advanced at a conference by scholars from Chinese institutions, such as the School of International Studies at Jinan University and the Center for South China Sea History and Culture at the National Institute for South China Sea Studies.

It may not be surprising that China claiming Philippine territory has been an object of anger. There are already tensions between China and the Philippines regarding maritime territory in the South China Sea, affecting fishing grounds.

Interestingly, such claims over Batanes are made on the basis of the claim that Batanes is a feature of Taiwan. If China claims Taiwan to be part of its territory, then, by virtue of this claim, Batanes would also be part of China.

In June, 60 Tao residents of Orchid Island set out on a voyage to Batanes onboard a wooden plank vessel, retracing a migration and trade route used by their ancestors. The voyage highlighted the strong historical and cultural connections between the Indigenous Tao residents of Orchid Island, also known as Lanyu, and Batanes. Apart from clear linguistic links, mythological tales point toward the historical link between the two islands.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Will New Laws Prevent Another “Grand Canyon of Meinong”?
content:
NEW LAWS PASSED by the legislature stiffen penalties for illegal gravel mining. Under the new provisions, mining without a permit for profit can result in a term of up to five years in prison and a fine of up to 500 million NT. Those who then do not restore gravel mining sites can face repeated fines of 100,000 NT to 2.5 million NT.

Mining activities that result in a disaster can result in fines of up to 60 million NT and one to seven years in prison, while mining activities that result in serious injury lead to three to ten years in prison and up to 80 million NT in fines. Finally, mining activities that lead to death can be punished by a minimum of seven years in jail to life imprisonment and fines of 100 million NT.

The new laws are a reaction to a mining case last year in Meinong, referred to in the media as the “Grand Canyon of Meinong.”

With regard to the case, gravel pits were found to be covering six hectares of land, with one pit being twenty meters deep. Prosecutors estimated that 1.3 million cubic meters of gravel was removed and sold to construction companies, for a profit of 300 million NT.

The owners of the land attempted to conceal the illegal mining operation by filling the pits with waste, which included construction materials and industrial waste. This proved a means of further exploiting the land, in that they charged for this means of waste disposal.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Recent Incident Highlights Use of Chinese Parts in Biometric Equipment in Police, Coast Guard, and Customs
content:
DPP LEGISLATOR Lin Chun-hsian publicized earlier this month that the police, coast guard, customs, and CPC Corporation are all suspected of using equipment of Chinese manufacture in biometric equipment. Such equipment was used for clocking in employees using their faces and fingerprints.

Such equipment is originally thought to be manufactured by ARMATURA, a subsidiary of ZKTeco, which is 99.98% owned by ZKTeco. That it ended up in police, coast guard, customs, and CPC use is because a Taiwanese company is suspected of rebranding and reselling the equipment. The NCC certification data for the devices, as well as their product descriptions, are identical to ARMATURA products. The instruction manual for the products, too, retains terms used in China but not Taiwan.

Reportedly, such purchases of equipment took place across a decade, with the Taiwanese company in question winning 16 tenders. Lin has called for a review of the procurement process, suggesting that designated government agencies should not be allowed to decide on purchases of equipment that store biometric or other sensitive data. Lin has also suggested an issue with the current procurement process, in that even equipment pertaining to national security must go to the lowest bidder, meaning that this incentivizes the purchase of what may be Chinese equipment.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Ma Wen-chun Again Accused of Leaking Confidential Details About Taiwanese Military
content:
THE MINISTRY OF NATIONAL DEFENSE (MND) has announced plans to domestically manufacture explosives. Specifically, the MND intends to produce RDX, or hexogen, in Taiwan. RDX is used in bombs, grenades, shells, and other explosive ordnance, including Composition B, PBXN-109, and TNT.

That the MND intends to domestically manufacture RDX can be seen as a move toward greater self-reliance. Similarly, Taiwan has announced plans to boost domestic production of shells and missiles.

Nevertheless, the reason as to why the MND intends to domestically manufacture RDX rather than import it is noteworthy. According to the MND, KMT legislator Ma Wen-chun, the co-chair of the defense committee in the legislature, had scuppered Taiwan’s plans to acquire RDX through purchase from India by exporting it through the Home-Max Furniture Trading Company.

Ma did this by revealing India as the country that Taiwan intended to purchase RDX from, with only the US, China, and India being the only countries in the world that manufacture RDX at scale. Reportedly, this opened the way for Chinese political interference directed at India.

For her part, Ma has denied that her revealing India as the country that Taiwan intended to purchase from was significant. But this is not the first time that Ma has been accused of leaking confidential details about the Taiwanese military.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Why Has China Targeted Educators with Sponsored Trips to Xinjiang?
content:
CONTROVERSY HAS broken out after news reports of Chinese United Front outreach to Taiwanese teachers.

In particular, the trips would have brought Taiwanese teachers to Xinjiang for an eight-day, seven-night trip with all expenses paid, outside of a 4,000 NT fee.

Among the stops on the trip would have been Xinjiang’s capital of Urumqi, as well as several educational institutions. This would include a vocational school in Beitun, as well as Shihezi University. Xinjiang Want Want Foods would also be a stop, with Taiwan’s Want Want Group known for its pro-unification stances, and its efforts to advance such views in Taiwan through media outlets it acquired in past years such as the China Times and CtiTV. Want Want Group founder Tsai Eng-meng has made no secret of the fact that his aim in acquiring such outlets was to promote positive views of China in Taiwan.

The Mainland Affairs Council has framed China as aiming to establish “nodes” in which teachers can propagate pro-CCP talking points. Indeed, one notes that subsidized trips to China are a long-established tactic of China’s United Front, aiming to extoll the benefits that Taiwanese could receive with unification. Of course, the version of China that Taiwanese are taken to see is a highly curated one, designed to convey positive perceptions.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Anger Breaks Out Against Fu Kun-chi After Protester Removed from Hualien Harvest Festival
content:
OUTRAGE HAS BROKEN out after online clips began to circulate of a protester against the Harvest Festival in Hualien who was removed by police, despite only silently holding up a sign.

In particular, the Harvest Festival is among the most important annual events for many Indigenous communities in Taiwan. The protester in question, who was wearing Amis traditional clothing, identified himself as also being Amis.

Specifically, however, the man’s protest was against the commodification of Indigenous culture in the Harvest Festival for consumption by tourists. This was criticized as an act that occurred under the political rule of Hualien legislator Fu Kun-chi and his wife, Hualien County Magistrate Hsu Cheng-wei.

The circumstances and pretext by which the man was removed from the Harvest Festival were further angering. Namely, the man was carrying a knife, which is a part of traditional Amis clothing. The man was questioned by police over carrying this knife and as to whether he was genuinely Indigenous and, in this way, having the legal cultural rights to carry the knife without it being considered a weapon. That the man’s arrest took place in this way seemed to drive home the point of Indigenous cultural events being commodified at the hands of the KMT political dynasty represented by Fu and Hsu.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Is the AI Boom Contributing to Rampant Speculation in Taiwan?
content:
RECENT REPORTS in international media have highlighted concern over Taiwanese taking out loans in order to pay for tech stocks. Specifically, it may be that the current growth in the tech sector in Taiwan, especially over the AI boom, is pushing young Taiwanese to take out loans with the belief that the tech sector will continually rise.

This is especially concerning when the current wave of growth in the economy, as driven primarily by AI, cannot last indefinitely. It is probable that the world will see a global impact similar to that of the dot-com bubble from the eventual bursting of the AI bubble, even if AI–as with the Internet–as a whole will continue to be influential as a technology, once investors realize that AI has not sufficiently found a way to monetize.

There have been waves of speculation in Taiwan in the past. During the authoritarian period, floating capital would end up diverted into the national lottery. Consequently, people would sink vast sums of money into lottery tickets, and the announcing of lottery numbers would see a great deal of public attention each day.

author: Brian Hioe
title: History First as Tragedy, Then as Blob: The Taiwan Labor Party on Taiwan’s History in the Tricontinental Institute
content:
by Brian Hioe
語言:
English
Photo Credit: Screenshot
History as Indistinguishable, Homogeneous Blob
IN THE WAKE of a letter by a Taiwanese academic that claimed Taiwan and China were part of the same polity…based on a land bridge that connected the two during the Ice Age, Vijay Prashad’s Tricontinental Institute has now followed up with a lengthy piece by Zang Ruxing. Zang is the director of the International Department of the Taiwan Labor Party. The piece, entitled “The Taiwan Question: From Civil War to External Intervention,” proves remarkable for many reasons, least of which is that the piece is dead on arrival from the first paragraph. Zang writes:
“Taiwan and the mainland are part of one and the same China. They have never been divided by any historical boundary. The people of Taiwan and the people of the Chinese mainland are one nation, with no division between them: they share the same language, the same history and culture, and the same folk-religious traditions.”
Indeed, if Taiwan and China have never been divided, one wonders why there is talk of the need to combat “independence” or achieve “unification” in the many paragraphs that follow. author: Brian Hioe
title: Is the Number of Taiwanese Missing in China Increasing?
content:
by Brian Hioe
語言:
English
Photo Credit: Picrazy2/WikiCommons/CC BY-SA 4.0
ACCORDING TO THE Mainland Affairs Council (MAC), earlier this month, ten Taiwanese were reported missing in China the same week by family members.
Likewise, the MAC has stated that the number of Taiwanese who have disappeared in China has sharply increased in the past two years. While 55 Taiwanese were reported missing in 2024, this increased to 221 last year. Just in 2026 alone, 109 cases have already been reported.
Of the ten Taiwanese who disappeared earlier this month, one had traveled to visit family, one for work, and four others for unknown reasons. On the other hand, according to the MAC, of the 385 disappeared Taiwanese, 30 are known to be under detention, 198 are known to have had their personal freedoms restricted, and 157 have simply vanished without contact.
It is, of course, not impossible that some of the disappeared Taiwanese experienced accidents or deliberately cut off contact with friends and family. Nevertheless, in recent memory, there have also been more cases reported of Taiwanese who have been questioned by Chinese public security officials.

author: Helen Li
title: Hong Kong Diaspora Recreate New and Old Traditions to Keep Memories Alive
content:
by Helen Li
語言:
English
Photo Credit: Taiwan Association for Human Rights/Facebook
IN THE RAINY darkness of Taipei’s 228 Memorial Park’s amphitheatre, echoes of songs rang out.
Mr. L stood there handing out flyers. On the back of the paper holding lyrics to the song《祭英烈》or ”Remember the Martyrs,” by Lo Kwok-cheung, a Hong Kong social movement song sung each year in Victoria Park.
“My mother tongue is Cantonese. It’s very hard to find an all-Cantonese-speaking event in Taipei,” the 37-year-old said.
For the past decade, every June 4th has brought a vigil near Taipei’s Chiang Kai-Shek Memorial Hall. During the last two years, there has been another event organized by the Hong Kong diaspora in Taipei. While there is comfort in solidarity standing up onstage with the Taipei vigil organizers at CKS, there’s a certain familiarity at the 228 Memorial Park that they can’t find elsewhere.
“There’s another gathering, but to a Hong Konger, this one has its own special meaning,” Mr. L said. For the twenty or so people who attended, it was a continuation of a ritual that has all but disappeared. The two gatherings at the Chiang Kai-Shek Memorial and 228 now occur annually in Taipei. However, there are other non-June 4th monthly or so gatherings sponsored by various Cantonese-language specific associations around the city.
